newsitem.title: USA: USDA offers help for Dakota, Minnesota farmers.
newsitem.headline: USDA offers help for Dakota, Minnesota farmers.

text.p: The Agriculture Department said on Tuesday that flood-damaged farms in the Dakotas and Minnesota could qualify for a variety of crop loans and other assistance.
More than 90 percent of eligible farm land in North and South Dakota is covered by federal crop insurance, Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said in a statement released in Washington.

Glickman travelled to Grand Forks, N.D., on Tuesday with President Clinton and several other cabinet members to survey extensive damage from the Red River. The Clinton administration is seeking some $488 million worth of disaster assistance for rural and urban damage to the three states.
North Dakota farmers have an estimated 1.7 million acres under water and much of that flooded acreage will not be planted this season, state officials said earlier this week.
The USDA said it was evaluating the Conservation Reserve Program, farm operating loans and other disaster assistance programs to help farmers.

Farmers in flood-ravaged counties that are declared disaster areas can receive low-interest USDA loans, the agency said. Some may also qualify for the agency's emergency conservation program that pays farmers to restore land to its productive capacity by removing debris and rebuilding fences.
Rural communities with sewage or water systems damaged by the flood can apply for assistance from the USDA's Rural Utilities Service.
"USDA stands ready to help in any way possible," Glickman said. "One of USDA's top priorities is always to ensure that no one goes hungry as a result of a natural disaster."

In North Dakota, the agency has provided some 38,000 pounds of fruits, vegetables and meat for emergency meal service to families evacuated from their homes. The USDA gave the state permission to release other agency foods to disaster relief agencies and to use school lunch program inventories if needed.

Glickman also said the agency approved a request by North Dakota to operate an emergency food stamp program in eight counties. Other emergency food stamps may be issued once damage assessments are completed.
In Minnesota, about 40,000 pounds of USDA commodities valued at $45,000 were given to emergency shelters, and six counties were approved for emergency food stamp programs, the USDA said.
